claims.text: Overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation are governed by formation of a stable, coherent surface oxide layer.
The substrate's thermal expansion and mechanical properties influence the surface oxide layer.
The baseline coating is 10 μm thick and has a surface roughness of 0.1 μm.
The intervention increases coating thickness from 10 μm to 20 μm while maintaining the same substrate material.
Surface roughness will additionally be varied from the 0.1 μm baseline to 0.05 μm and 0.2 μm.
Coating thickness and surface roughness affect oxide-layer formation and stability.
The relevant operating regime is 500–700°C at a sliding speed of 1 m/s and a normal load of 10 N.
The stable coherent surface oxide consists of Cr2O3 and NiO.
The oxide layer is 100 nm thick and has a grain size of 50 nm.
The oxide layer impedes dislocation glide and crack propagation.
The oxide layer reduces surface stress concentration.
Reduced dislocation density and crack growth rate lead to a 30% reduction in wear and deformation.
The modified coating will reduce wear rate by 25%, from 1×10^-4 to 7.5×10^-5 mm^3/Nm.
The modified coating will reduce microscopic deformation by 20%, from 0.1 μm to 0.08 μm.
Microscopic deformation can be represented by average surface roughness and scratch depth.
The predicted reductions should hold between 500°C and 700°C.
The magnitudes of the reductions depend on substrate properties, coating microstructure, and coating defects.
Failure to achieve at least a 20% wear-rate reduction and a 15% microscopic-deformation reduction relative to the 10 μm control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The mechanism states a 30% reduction in both wear and deformation, whereas the predicted outcome specifies a 25% wear reduction and a 20% deformation reduction.
The value 0.1 μm is introduced as baseline surface roughness but is later treated as baseline microscopic deformation and as both roughness and scratch depth, conflating distinct measurements.
